extracted.intended_audience: general readers of classic literature (Don Quixote)
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from Cervantes' Don Quixote containing narrative scenes (romantic reconciliation, inn episode) and an extended discourse comparing the merits of arms and letters; mixes plot action with ethical and philosophical argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: True nobility consists in virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: "true nobility consists in virtue" (not merely blood); one who lacks virtue cannot claim higher nobility by birth alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as Dorothea's argument to deny lineage-based superiority: virtue, not blood, is the core of nobility; examples/appeal to conscience follow — if one refuses justice to another, the claimant cannot rightly boast of nobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep plighted word / faithfulness to promises
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping one’s pledge is required of a gentleman and Christian; a plighted word should not and ought not to be false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curate and others urge Don Fernando that he must keep his promise, that doing so obeys God and gains approval of sensible people; keeping pledges is a test of honour, Christianity, and gentlemanly conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience as arbiter of truth and reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscience will 'lift up its silent voice' and vindicate truth, undermining the pleasure of those who act wrongly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dorothea warns that even if human witnesses fail, one’s own conscience will testify and 'mar thy highest pleasure and enjoyment' — conscience is invoked as a moral standard and ultimate judge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generosity, magnanimity, and restraint in the face of passion
rubrics_metrics.description: When passion asserts itself, a generous, reasoned mind should conquer impulse; it is becoming to show forbearance rather than vengeance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speakers urge Don Fernando to 'show a generous mind' and to 'conquer and put a constraint upon himself' so that reason prevails over passion, allowing lovers to live in peace; rejecting vengeance is held as noble behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue and modesty elevate social standing
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty combined with modesty and 'the surpassing love she bore him' can raise a woman of humble birth to equality with a gentleman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument presented to Don Fernando: that beauty plus virtue and modesty make it proper for a gentleman to accept a lover of lower birth without slur, showing that personal qualities can justify social elevation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure passion without sin is not blameworthy
rubrics_metrics.description: "when the potent sway of passion asserts itself, so long as there be no mixture of sin in it, he is not to be blamed who gives way to it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mitigates moral condemnation: natural passion, if free of sin, can be forgiven or understood — used to counsel leniency toward lovers whose feelings are sincere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate a calling by its end/goal
rubrics_metrics.description: "The end and goal that each seeks to attain" is the proper measure of which calling (arms or letters) is more estimable; the nobler the object of the calling, the more estimable it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don Quixote argues that arms aim at peace (the highest good) while letters aim at distributive justice; therefore, by their ends, arms are superior. Use purpose/outcome as a criterion when comparing vocations or activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peace as the supreme aim (arms’ justification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peace is 'the true end of war' and 'the greatest boon that men can desire in this life'; because arms aim to secure peace, their purpose is nobler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don Quixote repeatedly emphasizes that war/arms should be judged by their aim to produce peace; the moral value of arms stems from this ultimate purpose rather than the violence entailed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters aim to establish distributive justice and good laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of human letters 'is to establish distributive justice, give to every man that which is his, and see and take care that good laws are observed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters are defended as pursuing a noble, lofty aim (distinct from divine letters), namely justice and lawful order; when weighing worth, consider the societal role of education and law-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost/effort as measure of value
rubrics_metrics.description: What 'costs most is valued and deserves to be valued most' — the greater sacrifices and risks incurred in a calling increase its claim to esteem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don Quixote compares students' poverty and hardships to soldiers' harsher poverty and constant risk of death, using suffering and danger as a metric for the relative value of the professions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare material hardships concretely
rubrics_metrics.description: Students endure poverty, hunger, cold, thin garments, and other privations; soldiers endure the same and far greater risks, including near-certain danger in battle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The discourse itemizes concrete hardships ("hunger, or cold, or nakedness... want of shirts..." vs. soldiers' exposure, slashed doublets, sleeping on the ground, risk of mines/battle wounds) as evidence supporting claims about relative merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligence/mental exertion required by arms
rubrics_metrics.description: Arms require high intelligence as much as letters: 'acts of vigour for the execution of which high intelligence is requisite' — military conduct involves planning, stratagems, and mind as well as body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to rebut the claim that letters are intellectually superior: military success depends on mental faculties (anticipating enemy plans, countermeasures), so intellectual demands should not be used to disqualify arms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual dependence of arms and letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters argue that without them arms cannot maintain themselves (laws govern war); arms argue that without them laws and states cannot be maintained — both are interdependent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text acknowledges the reciprocal role: laws (letters) regulate war, while arms enforce and protect the conditions under which law and society function; any evaluation should account for this interdependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of rewarding soldiers vs scholars
rubrics_metrics.description: It is harder to reward soldiers: many perish and those who survive are few and often poorly recompensed; men of letters more readily find modest means of support ('by skirts... they all find means of support').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don Quixote uses the practical difficulty of rewarding soldiers as a counterargument to valuing arms by cost: even though soldiers endure more, their social/economic reward is limited, complicating simple valuation-by-sacrifice.
